title.zh: 「我們永遠不走」：被預言沉入海中的北極村落，用一首歌改寫氣候政治
title.en: "We'll Never Go": How Inuit Youth Refused the Script of Climate Disappearance

summary.zh:
【總結】這篇發表於《Political Geography》的論文，由因紐特青年與南方學者共同執筆，核心是一部名為《Don't Give Up》的音樂影片。位於加拿大北極海岸、僅約900人的圖克托亞圖克（Tuktoyaktuk），長年被媒體與氣候科學描繪為「正在墜入海洋的村莊」，甚至被預言2050年將不再適合居住。但當地青年創作的歌詞卻唱著：「不、不、不，沒有更好的地方（我們住在這裡），我們永遠不走。」作者指出，這不是否認氣候變遷，而是一種「拒絕的政治」——拒絕被寫成等待救援的受害者，拒絕把遷徙當成唯一結局。研究的突破在於：把一首歌當作嚴肅的主權政治文本，證明拒絕可以是歡慶的、旋律性的、集體的，而非沉默或否定。

【研究問題】文章追問：主流氣候論述在「拯救」北極社區時，是否正複製殖民邏輯？過去研究的盲點在於，媒體與政策慣以「脆弱性」框架描寫因紐特人：CBC報導海岸線每年流失一米、《華盛頓郵報》形容村莊會「像鹽溶於水般消散」、BBC（每週觸及4.92億觀眾）稱之為「幾乎被遺忘的原住民生活方式」。這些敘事把人與侵蝕的沉積物混為一談，抹去了能動性。作者將此追溯到1950年代的「北極遷移計畫」：加拿大政府以「更好的生活」為名，把因紐特家庭從Inukjuak與Pond Inlet遷往荒蕪的高緯度地區，實際目的是冷戰時期宣示主權，結果造成飢餓與創傷，皇家委員會事後確認政府從未取得知情同意。作者主張，今日的「氣候搬遷」論述正在重演這種「定居者未來主義」——因紐特的未來被預先寫成消失，除非國家出手相救。

【研究方法】方法上的亮點是「歌詞引導法」（lyric-elicitation），整個研究由因紐特青年主導，遵循《國家因紐特研究策略》對研究設計、詮釋與傳播的治理要求。2025年春天，共同作者兼作詞者Carmen Kuptana在當地Mangilaluk學校主持工作坊：她把整首歌詞寫在大張紙上，邀請14至24歲的參與者用便利貼在自己的歌詞旁註解、討論。這個方法植基於因紐特知識傳統unipkait——視生動的口述、具身與藝術性敘事為知識本身。非因紐特合作者僅在受邀下提供理論與編輯協助，最終分析權與定稿權都在青年手中。選擇匿名的青年以化名呈現，署名者則以真名現身——這是一套以集體所有權為本的倫理，而非知識榨取。這種「以口述素養為方法」的設計，本身就是對政治地理學慣用文本分析與訪談的傳統的挑戰。

【結果】三大關鍵發現。其一，青年把「侵蝕」複數化：Logan註解「所有這些侵蝕／我情緒爆發」，指出侵蝕不只是海岸退縮，還包括殖民創傷、心理健康與文化壓力；Willow的歌詞「壞記憶像船漂浮」指向曾載孩子去寄宿學校的Lourdes船——環境與歷史的傷口被一併命名。其二，「我們得留下」不是感傷，而是對「留下權」的主權宣示，呼應Simpson所謂原住民的「扎根規範性」；反覆的「不、不、不」不是關閉對話，而是騰出空間，按自己的條件生活。其三，拒絕以「在場」演出：影片裡青年跳舞、串珠、擊鼓、狩獵，正如一位青年所寫：「我們不只是倖存，我們是生活在這裡。」這對遷移研究提出「自願不遷移」的政治面向，對調適政策則表明：搬遷並非必然結局，也為去殖民化研究方法立下範例。
summary.en:
**Summary:** This Political Geography article, co-authored by Inuvialuit youth and southern academics, centres on a music video—"Don't Give Up"—written and performed by teenagers in Tuktoyaktuk, a hamlet of roughly 900 on Canada's Arctic coast. News media and climate science routinely script the community's demise: "the Arctic community falling into the ocean," predicted to be uninhabitable by 2050 as thawing permafrost surrenders up to a metre of coastline each year. Yet the youth's chorus insists otherwise: "No, no, no, there's no better place (WE LIVE HERE) and we'll never go." The authors argue this is not climate denial but climate politics—a refusal of the victimhood assigned to them and of relocation as the presumed endpoint. The breakthrough is both theoretical and methodological: treating a song as a sovereign political text, and showing that refusal can be joyful, melodic, and collective rather than silent or negational.

**Problem:** The article asks whether climate narratives that aim to "save" Arctic communities reproduce colonial logic even as they profess concern. The gap: media and policy habitually frame Inuit through vulnerability—CBC reports the hamlet "collapsing into the ocean," the Washington Post imagines it dissolving "like salt in water," and the BBC, reaching 492 million people weekly, describes an "almost-forgotten way of indigenous life" on "unremittingly spartan tundra." Such accounts conflate Inuit lives with eroding sediment, rendering them passive and almost already gone. The authors trace this framing to the 1950s Arctic Relocation Plan, when Canada moved Inuit families from Inukjuak and Pond Inlet to the barren High Arctic—officially for a "better life," actually to assert Cold War sovereignty—producing starvation and trauma; the Royal Commission later concluded no genuine informed consent was obtained. Today's "climate relocation" discourse, they contend, recycles this "settler futurity": Inuit futures foreclosed unless the state rescues them.

**Approach:** The study's centrepiece is "lyric-elicitation," a method designed and led by Inuvialuit youth in line with the National Inuit Strategy on Research, which mandates Inuit governance over research design, interpretation, and dissemination. In spring 2025, co-author and lyricist Carmen Kuptana hosted a workshop at Mangilaluk School: she wrote the video's lyrics on large sheets of paper and invited participants aged 14–24 to annotate and debate their own words using sticky notes. The method builds on unipkait, an Inuit knowledge practice that treats vivid oral, embodied, and artful storytelling as legitimate political knowledge. Non-Inuit collaborators contributed theory and editing only by invitation; final analytical and editorial decisions rested with the youth. Participants who chose anonymity appear under pseudonyms, while named co-authors claimed authorship on their own terms—an ethics of collective ownership rather than extraction.

**Results:** Three findings stand out. First, youth pluralized "erosion": Logan annotated "All these erosions/I'm exploding with emotion," naming colonial legacies, mental health struggles, and cultural pressures alongside coastal retreat; Willow's verse about a boat evoked the Lourdes vessel once used to transport children to residential schools—environmental and historical wounds named together. Second, "we gotta stay" operates as a demand, a sovereign right to remain echoing Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's "grounded normativity"; the insistent "no, no, no" clears space for life on Inuit terms rather than closing conversation. Third, refusal is performed through presence—dancing, beading, drumming, hunting—as one youth put it: "We're not just surviving here, we're living here." The implications ripple outward: for migration studies, "voluntary immobility" as political agency; for adaptation policy, proof that relocation is not inevitable; for methodology, lyric-elicitation as a template for decolonial, arts-based research.

keyArticle.title: “We'll never go”: Inuit youth refusals as climate politics
